newsitem.title: CHINA: Blood will stain Deng's historical mystique.
newsitem.headline: Blood will stain Deng's historical mystique.

text.p: For bereaved parents of unarmed students killed by the bullets and tanks of an army sent to crush their peaceful pro-democracy protests in 1989, Deng Xiaoping must be found guilty -- even after death.

"When I first learned about Deng Xiaoping's death, I got out of bed and burned incense... to appease my son's soul in heaven," said Ding Zilin, whose son Jiang Jielian, a high school student, was just 17 when he was killed on the night of June 3-4, 1989.

"This is all a mother could do at this moment," said Ding, an associate professor of philosophy at Beijing's People's University who has published a book containing the names of 150 victims of the bloody military crackdown.

Ding and other relatives of the hundreds of unarmed protesters killed on that balmy summer night say they still want a reckoning with the man who, as China's paramount leader, ordered the People's Liberation Army to open fire on the student-led demonstrations.

"What kind of responsibility must Deng Xiaoping bear in this massacre? This is something the government authorities cannot evade," she said. "I hope the Chinese authorities will muster the courage at an early date to face this."
Ding said she was surprised at how calmly she had reacted to the news that Deng, 92, had died last Wednesday after ruling China for 18 years. He was being cremated on Monday.
"If Deng Xiaoping had died one or two years after my son died in 1989, I would not have been this calm," she said. "Eight years have passed. My tears are almost dry."
But the bereaved still want an official review of what happened to ensure that their sons and daughters do not spend eternity officially vilified as criminals who sought to overthrow the state.
"It is an undeniable fact, if Deng Xiaoping had not given the order... there was no second ruler in China who dared to order martial law troops to open fire at civilians," Ding said.
"China is a society ruled by man not by law... he gave an order and people below him obeyed and the massacre happened."

China justifies its bloody crackdown on the student demonstrations, when hundreds were gunned down or crushed under the treads of advancing tanks, saying the protests and rallies that swept across the country were a counter-revolutionary rebellion.

"I think June 4 will not be forgotten," said a relative of Wang Dan, jailed for four years as a leader of the 1989 demonstrations and re-imprisoned last year to serve 11 years on charges of plotting against the state.
"From an historical perspective, I think it cannot be forgiven," the relative said of Deng's decision.
Deng never showed any sign of remorse for what is regarded as the bloodiest episode of his career.

However, his children, who reportedly tried to dissuade him in 1989 from using force, have hinted privately that they expect official history to review the current verdict on the Tiananmen massacre and add a bloody stain to their father's reputation.
"Judgement cannot be passed on Deng Xiaoping merely on his contributions and mistakes," Ding said. "Guilt should be added. The June 4 massacre is his guilt, not just a mistake."

Deng himself altered the historical verdict on Chairman Mao Zedong, whose Great Leap Forward and ultra-leftist 1966-76 Cultural Revolution killed millions, to describe his legacy as 70 percent good and 30 percent mistakes.
"It's too early to pass final judgement on Deng Xiaoping -- his contributions and his mistakes," Ding said. "I'm afraid the wounds brought to the country will not heal for generations."
